brief-1.text: Internal numeric contradiction in the capacity paragraph: at 2 hours 20 minutes per round trip, 6 round trips need 14 hours, but the harbours are open only 12 hours (07:00-19:00). The Calloway can make at most 5 round trips, so 2,000 seats each way, not 2,400 (the same timing is what limits today's two boats to 5 trips each, 1,200 seats). A strong reply flags the impossible sixth trip and corrects the figure.

Circular demand argument: the 1,500-a-day forecast is derived from assuming the Calloway's extra capacity gets filled, and that forecast is then used as the reason a ship of her size is needed. A strong reply names the circle and notes the forecast needs independent evidence (e.g. counts of turned-away passengers).

Sunk-cost reasoning: the £1.2 million already spent on the pier is gone whichever ship is chosen and cannot justify buying the Calloway. A strong reply says the pier spend is irrelevant to the decision (at most its future usefulness counts).

The conclusion answers an easier question ('is the Calloway the better ship?') instead of the one asked ('will the island be at least as well served through the winter?', with the council's 24-hour rule). The paper ignores the user's own fact that every vessel needs a three-week statutory dry-dock refit each winter: with a single ship the island gets no sailings for about three weeks, breaching the 24-hour condition, and there is no backup if she breaks down. A strong reply says that, as proposed, the answer to the user's question is no unless relief cover (a chartered or retained vessel) is arranged.

brief-2.text: Selection bias: the 6% churn belongs to clinics that chose the annual plan, a self-selected, more committed group. Forcing monthly clinics onto annual does not give them that group's churn. A strong reply says the 6% cannot be applied to the whole base.

Numeric contradiction: the note's own test shows 212 of 360 clinics (about 59%) accepting annual-only, yet it concludes that at least 95% of monthly clinics will switch 'on that evidence'. The evidence implies roughly 41% refusing. A strong reply flags the gap between 59% and 95%.

Circular argument: clinics that leave are defined as 'never committed', so their loss is ruled not to count; the conclusion that no real revenue is lost is built into the definition. It also contradicts the stated 25% annual monthly churn, which means about three-quarters of these clinics would otherwise have stayed the year. A strong reply names the circularity and counts those departures as real losses.

The conclusion answers an easier question (are annual clinics more valuable per customer?) instead of the board's (will total recurring revenue a year out be higher than with no change?). Each switching clinic pays £900 instead of £1,080, a 17% cut. With no change, a year out is about £943k (820 x 0.75 x £1,080 + 330 x 0.94 x £900); even granting 6% churn, the change only breaks even if about 96% of monthly clinics switch, and at the test's 59% it falls to about £688k. A strong reply concludes the answer is likely no on the note's own figures.

brief-3.text: Availability bias: one memorable incident (the Corran Mill fire, 14 minutes) is used to say Eastfield station has served the estates poorly, while the user's own fact is that it meets the 8-minute standard on 93% of calls. A strong reply says the single incident does not outweigh the record.

Circular validation: the model's road speeds were set to reproduce the times expected from a ring-road site like Harrow Cross, and the model is then cited as confirming that Harrow Cross meets the standard. The output was tuned to the conclusion. A strong reply says the model needs calibration against actual recorded response times.

Arithmetic contradiction: 5.6 km at 48 km/h is 7 minutes, not 5; with 90 seconds' turnout that is 8 minutes 30 seconds, outside the 8-minute standard, and that is only to the centre of the estates, at average speed. A strong reply corrects the figure and says the paper's own numbers fail the standard.

The conclusion answers an easier question (does the borough-wide average response time improve?) instead of the one asked (will Eastfield get a first engine within 8 minutes on at least 90% of calls?). A borough average can improve while one district gets worse, and an average says nothing about the 90th percentile. A strong reply says the paper does not answer the question and that an Eastfield-specific percentile figure is needed.
